item.title: How Criminal Gangs Are Stealing Homes in Mexico City
item.author: Bloomberg Originals
item.content:encoded:
In Mexico City, housing theft happens on average 11 times a day, often when homeowners are on vacation or have died, leaving properties vacant. In many cases criminal gangs move in, claiming ownership in an effort to profit from a gentrification wave that’s boosted home prices.
Many such “dispossessions” can involve title fraud and even complicit public officials. Mexico City recorded 2,676 cases this year through August, according to public records, bringing the total over the past decade to nearly 41,000.
The sheer number of incidents lays bare two key problems for President Claudia Sheinbaum: security and the cost of living. While homicides have plunged under her watch, reports of extortion are at their highest in more than a decade. She also has made expanding access to affordable homes a national priority, yet nowhere is the challenge more stark than the capital, where protests frequently break out over evictions and rising foreign demand.

item.title: Between Capitol Hill and Black Broadway - Washington, D.C.'s hidden worlds | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Barely a day goes by without images of Washington, D.C. being in the media. The US capital is the nation's political heart, and its iconic landmarks exude a sense of history.
Washington's monuments and memorials are known around the world. They tell the story of the United States, from the White House to the Capitol and the Lincoln Memorial, where Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his famous "I Have a Dream" speech.
But proximity to the corridors of power is just one reason for the city's appeal. Away from the monumental avenues and boulevards lies a vibrant cultural scene that dances to the beat of go-go. The genre, created by local African American musicians, still fills the funk clubs on what's known as "Black Broadway" in the U Street neighborhood.
Washington is a city of contrasts. In the 1970s, its nonwhite majority population gave it the nickname "Chocolate City." It's a place where people of all kinds try to realize humanity's greatest ideas: freedom, equality, democracy and human rights. D.C. is a political idea, carved in the marble of its monuments. And yet behind its famous facades, the city has more to offer than many realize.

item.title: How Do Fungi Keep the Planet Healthy? | PODCAST: The Joy of Why
item.author: Quanta Magazine
item.content:encoded:
Evolutionary biologist Toby Kiers explains how fungal networks in soil trade nutrients with plants, help keep carbon underground, and strike bargains without having a brain.
“The Joy of Why” is a Quanta Magazine podcast about curiosity and the pursuit of knowledge. The mathematician and author Steven Strogatz and the cosmologist and author Janna Levin take turns interviewing leading researchers about the great scientific and mathematical questions of our time. For more episodes visit Quanta Magazine: https://www.quantamagazine.org/tag/the-joy-of-why/
---------
0:00 Introduction 2:42 What Are Mycorrhizal Fungi? 5:30 How Plants and Fungi Trade Resources 8:00 Inside the Underground Fungal Network 11:30 How Fungi Shape Climate and Ecosystems 16:05 The Underground Marketplace: Cooperation and Competition 26:15 How Fungi Make Decisions Without Brains 29:40 The Hidden Partnership Between Fungi and Bacteria 34:14 Watching Nutrients Move Through Fungal Networks 40:28 Mapping and Protecting Earth's Underground Biodiversity 45:00 The Strange Biology of Fungi 49:35 What Fungi Reveal About Cooperation in Nature
---------
People may think of soil as just dirt, but it is anything but inert. Beneath your feet, a vast network of mycorrhizal fungi is hard at work, trading minerals with plant roots. This trading system helps enrich the soil, and it sequesters 13 billion tons of atmospheric carbon dioxide each year — roughly equivalent to one-third of the world’s fossil-fuel emissions. Scientists know that these fungi form partnerships with 80% of all plant species on Earth, a relationship that evolved some 450 million years ago. What they have not understood is how organisms with no brain or central nervous system can decide whom to trade with, and on what terms.
Toby Kiers, an evolutionary biologist at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, has spent much of her career making this hidden world visible. Drawing on economics and game theory, and using tools that range from fluorescent quantum dots to imaging robots, her lab is probing how fungi and plants conduct their trade. The work raises new questions about soil, carbon, and even what counts as an individual organism. In this episode, Kiers tells co-host Steven Strogatz how these brainless, decentralized organisms can behave strategically — discriminating between better and worse partners and shifting resources across the network to wherever a plant will “pay” more for it — and how she has built a worldwide community of researchers

item.title: The King Obsessed With Witches
item.author: History Hit
item.content:encoded:
Maddy Pelling and Anthony Delaney investigate one of Europe’s bloodiest witch hunts: Scotland’s North Berwick Witch trials of 1591. In this extraordinary case, fears escalated all the way up the social hierarchy to the King himself, James VI. A wild storm in the North Sea had nearly killed James and his new wife Anne of Denmark, fuelling his fascination with the intellectual study of demonology. A maelstrom of terror brought together the King’s paranoia of a conspiracy against him with local rivalries and misfortune, twisting together the fates of individuals from maidservants to magistrates, in the hunt for scapegoats.
Maddy and Anthony meet at Edinburgh’s Holyrood Palace, the place where the King himself interrogated one of the alleged witches, Agnes Sampson, a local healer and midwife. This was a remarkable moment when different worlds met, king and commoner, captured through the accounts of her confession.
But who were the accused, and how were their confessions extracted? Maddy and Anthony travel through this area of Scotland and examine the records to understand how the fear of witches spread through entire communities, and how the women and men of North Berwick were tragically caught up in the terror.

DESCRIPTION Matt Erman, a senior software engineer at Blackboard and author of “Grokking Software Architecture”, tells host Luca Mezzalira he wrote the book after mentoring junior developers who stared blankly at basic fundamentals, just as AI was raising the bar for entry-level jobs and junior hiring was dropping. His core thesis is that AI only amplifies what you are: it speeds up good developers and accelerates chaos for those without foundations. He argues architects should think of themselves as "clarity engineers", and the book's five-step process reflects that. Start with what you're being asked to build, ask why (the Toyota Five Whys) until you reach the real driver, sketch the design, and write the decision down, including what you are explicitly not optimizing for. There is no perfect solution, only the best one for your constraints (a three-person team with a two-week deadline shouldn't build a web of microservices). Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) keep teams from relitigating the same choice every few weeks, and communication matters because the best idea doesn't always win, the best-communicated one does.
On AI, Erman's warnings are specific. An engineer's value is moving up the chain, from writing code to directing, reviewing, and challenging agents, but skills erode if nobody writes or reads code anymore. The risk isn't that AI writes bad code. It knows every pattern ever created, and without clear constraints it can stitch them into "Frankenstein code" that works today and fails later. "AI told me to" is not a defensible answer in a PR review, and at AI speed you may make four or five architectural decisions in the time you once made one, so planning matters more, not less. He also explains Hyrum's Law: with enough users, every observable behavior of your API becomes a contract, documented or not. He doesn't expect AI to replace human judgment soon, because much of what matters about a system lives in context nobody has written down. His practical tip for newer developers is to always ask the AI for an adversarial, architect-level review of its own work. His advice for the next six months: step back and gain clarity before you write code (even a "favorites" button hides architectural decisions), and build things to last by separating concerns and keeping them modular. Luca adds that deterministic tools and probabilistic AI work best together.

item.title: North Korea's alliance with China and Russia | DW Documentary

item.content:encoded:
For decades, people have predicted the collapse of North Korea. Yet the Kim dynasty seems more entrenched than ever. Propaganda, military posturing and a nuclear program are shoring up Kim Jong Un's power, both domestically and internationally.
This documentary traces North Korea's evolution from an isolated hereditary dictatorship to a state whose nuclear weapons program is cause for global concern. Today, the regime possesses missiles capable of potentially reaching long-range targets. Meanwhile, it is also seeking closer ties with key partners China and Russia. And for the first time, North Korea is deploying thousands of soldiers to fight alongside Russia in its war in Ukraine — a conspicuous move that provides the country combat experience, foreign currency, and access to new military technology. Drawing on new archival sources, exclusive analysis from experts and insights into North Korea's elaborate propaganda machine, this documentary shows how the regime fosters loyalty and cements its power. A cult of personality, shows of military strength and foreign policy successes all serve to maintain its power at home. This underscores why Kim Jong Un currently sees himself in a strategically advantageous position — and why Pyongyang's role on the international stage is becoming increasingly significant. Despite being a small, largely isolated country, North Korea regularly finds itself at the center of geopolitical tensions. Three generations of the Kim dynasty have created a system of government based on control, isolation and military strength. What strategies have allowed the Kim family to continue ruling to this day — and what are the consequences for the region and the world?
